summary:
HEALTH-01 is a health monitoring tool for astronauts on long missions. It collects data from an iPhone, Apple Watch or Android phone, plus short daily check-ins, and shows heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, body temperature, sleep and mood for each crew member.

We didn’t use Earth norms. Research from NASA’s Human Research Program shows that heart rate, blood pressure and body temperature all change in microgravity, so the app compares each astronaut with their own in-flight baseline. When something drifts, it raises an alert that explains what changed and links to the NASA evidence behind it.

The models were trained and tested on real public wearable datasets from PhysioNet, PMData and Stanford. They spot fatigue, early signs of illness and changes in blood sugar. We also added Inspiration4 crew blood data from NASA OSDR. Cabin sensors send CO2, pressure and radiation readings over MQTT, and short tests based on NASA-TLX track workload and reaction time.

There’s also an assistant that crew can ask about their data. It’s a Qwen2.5 model we fine-tuned on NASA reports and open-access space medicine papers. It runs on local hardware, so it keeps working without a link to Earth, and every answer cites its source.

The point is simple: catch problems early, when the nearest doctor is months away.
details:
What it does

HEALTH-01 tracks astronaut health on long missions and warns the crew when something starts to go wrong. It reads data from an iPhone, Apple Watch or Android phone and from short daily check-ins. It shows the six indicators named in the challenge: heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, body temperature, sleep and mood. It also tracks HRV, steps, exercise, workload, fatigue and reaction time. Cabin sensors send CO2, pressure, humidity and radiation readings over MQTT, so the crew can see how their health and their environment affect each other.

How it works

NASA’s research shows that the body changes in space. In-flight heart rate and blood pressure are lower than before launch, core temperature rises by about 1 °C, and bones lose 1 to 1.5% of their mineral density each month. Earth reference ranges don’t fit an astronaut, so the app learns each person’s own in-flight baseline and flags changes from it. Each alert says what changed, why it matters and what NASA recommends, and links to the source report and page.

The models come in as plug-ins. They spot fatigue, early signs of illness from resting heart rate, and changes in blood sugar. We trained and tested them on real public wearable datasets (PMData, the Stanford smartwatch study, and CGMacros and MMASH from PhysioNet), because no public dataset has astronaut wearable data. The app also uses blood panels from the Inspiration4 crew, taken from NASA OSDR, as research context.

The assistant is a Qwen2.5 model that we fine-tuned with QLoRA on NASA Human Research Program reports and open-access space medicine papers. It runs on local hardware through Ollama, so it works without a connection to Earth. Every answer cites its source, and we built the training data only from real source sentences so the model has nothing made up to learn.

Benefits and impact

On a Mars mission a message can take up to 20 minutes each way, and there’s no doctor on board. The aim is to catch problems early, like sleep debt, heavy fatigue, a coming illness or slow weight loss, while they’re still easy to treat. Ground teams get a clear daily picture without the crew spending extra time on paperwork. The same tool would also work for people in remote stations, in polar bases or on submarines.

Tools and technology

  • Languages: Python, TypeScript, Swift and Kotlin
  • Backend: FastAPI, PostgreSQL, SQLAlchemy and Eclipse Mosquitto (MQTT)
  • Machine learning: scikit-learn and pandas; PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers, PEFT and TRL for fine-tuning
  • Assistant: Ollama
  • Web: React, Vite and Recharts
  • Phones: HealthKit on iPhone and Apple Watch, Health Connect on Android
  • Exercise: MediaPipe pose tracking in the browser counts reps from the camera
  • Hardware: iPhone, Apple Watch, iPad, Android phone and a GPU server on DigitalOcean for training and hosting

What makes it creative

Most health apps measure people against Earth averages. Ours compares each astronaut with their own in-flight baseline, using NASA’s numbers on how the body changes in space. Every claim the app makes links back to an exact quote in a NASA document; the build fails if a quote can’t be found in its source. The assistant runs fully offline. We also kept the interface hand-drawn and simple so it’s quick to read on a tablet.

What we considered

  • Honest data: Every value is labelled as real, research or simulated, and the app says plainly when a model was trained on Earth data and not on astronauts.
  • Privacy: The assistant only sees a crew member’s callsign, never their name or raw data. The camera doesn’t upload video unless the user gives clear consent.
  • Licences: We checked each dataset’s licence and used the stricter terms where sources disagreed.
  • Crew time: Check-ins take under a minute.
  • Offline use: Everything keeps working without a network.
  • Clear limits: Alerts are there to support the crew and flight surgeons. They don’t diagnose anything.
